title: The Dasam Granth question
hookLine: views differ on authorship of parts; devotion to Jaap and Chaupai is shared

lines: A SMALL BOOK ON A HIGH SHELF.
A SECOND GRANTH, A SECOND QUESTION.
cards: A gutka is a small prayer book, wrapped in cloth, kept on a high shelf. Open one that has been used for years and the paper tells on its owner.

Certain pages are softer than the rest, gray at the corners from thumbs, morning and evening. In some gutkas, two of those worn places are Jaap Sahib and Chaupai. Neither comes from the Guru Granth Sahib.
Both come from another book, the Dasam Granth, and that book carries one of the open questions of the panth.

teach.h: DASAM GRANTH: THE BOOK OF THE TENTH.
teach.b: Dasam Granth means the book of the Tenth, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. It is a large collection: hymns of praise, long retellings of old stories, poetry about battle, and the Zafarnama, a letter to the emperor.

teach.h: VIEWS DIFFER ON WHO WROTE WHICH PARTS.
teach.b: Here the views differ. Some Sikhs hold that the whole collection is the Guru's own work. Others hold that parts of it, especially some of the long story sections, came from poets who gathered at his court.
Others take a path between, accepting the prayers sung every day and studying the rest carefully. Scholars write books on it, and the conversation is sometimes heated. Now the part the sides share.
Jaap Sahib is a cascade of short, rhythmic lines praising the Timeless One. It opens, here in paraphrase, by describing God as having no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage.
Chaupai is a prayer asking God's protection, plain and personal.

teach.h: JAAP AND CHAUPAI: IN THE DAILY PRAYERS.
teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct places both among the daily prayers, the Nitnem: Jaap Sahib in the morning, Chaupai within the evening prayer. Both are recited when the amrit is prepared.
So Sikhs who disagree sharply about the book's edges recite the same lines, morning and evening.

teach.h: STUDY THE QUESTION, KEEP THE PRAYER.
teach.b: A question about authorship doesn't have to empty the prayer.

teach.h: NO MARK, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.
teach.b: People can keep studying a hard question and keep their thumbs on the same worn page.

how: Sikhs differ on the authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth, while Jaap Sahib and Chaupai, which the Rehat Maryada places in the daily Nitnem, are recited morning and evening, and both are recited when amrit is prepared.

games.q: two Sikhs disagree sharply about the authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth. what happens at the daily prayers?
o: both recite Jaap Sahib and Chaupai.
both stop praying until it's settled.
games.why: the debate is about the book's edges. the code places Jaap Sahib and Chaupai in the daily Nitnem, and devotion to them is shared.

practice: Bring up one question you carry that has no answer yet, about faith, family or what's true, and instead of gripping it, set it in an open palm; let your hand open on your knee if that helps.
Breathe in and let the question stay, breathe out and let it stop demanding a verdict today, and if you pray, rest on the Timeless One whom Jaap Sahib praises.
